What is Sandoval County, NM, and how big is it?

Sandoval County is the fourth-most populous county in New Mexico and part of the Albuquerque metropolitan area. Wikipedia reports 148,834 residents in the 2020 census, names Bernalillo as the county seat, and lists Rio Rancho as the other principal community.

The county was created in 1903 from the northern part of Bernalillo County, and its name comes from one of the large land-holding Spanish families in the area. It covers 3,716 square miles, and the highest point is the summit of Redondo Peak at 11,254 feet.

That geography produces two very different kinds of property: suburban lots in and around Rio Rancho, and larger rural or mountain parcels elsewhere in the county. Where a property sits determines which agencies appear on its tax bill.

What does Intel mean for Sandoval County?

Intel's Rio Rancho campus is the best-documented employer in the county. A 2021 press release from the governor's office said Intel planned a $3.5 billion investment and more than 700 new jobs at the site, and that the company had invested more than $16 billion in New Mexico since 1980.

The release quotes the county commission chair as saying the partnership began with a $2 billion industrial revenue bond in 1980 and has produced over 8,000 jobs, almost 5,000 of which went to New Mexico residents. It also says Intel spurred Rio Rancho's growth spurt in the 1980s.

These figures are from the 2021 announcement and are not current employment counts. For a house seller, the useful point is that a single large employer has shaped the Rio Rancho market for decades, and a Rio Rancho owner's sale timing can follow the local job market.

Who handles property tax in Sandoval County?

The Treasurer bills and collects, and the Assessor values. The county's Treasurer page gives the office at 1500 Idalia Road, Building D, Bernalillo, NM 87004, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Where does a Sandoval County tax dollar go?

Education takes the largest share. The Treasurer's chart for tax year 2025 shows 42 percent to education, 21 percent to municipal government, 20 percent to county government, 13 percent to the state, conservancy and other, and 5 percent to contracting hospitals.

The same page says the 2025 tax roll was $202.6 million, part of more than $1.483 billion the Treasurer is charged with collecting over ten years at a 99.22 percent collection rate. County programs funded include fire and 911, libraries, public safety, senior programs, roads, the landfill and the detention center. Where you live decides which agencies show up on your bill.

  • Education: 42 percent
  • Municipal government: 21 percent
  • County government: 20 percent
  • State, conservancy and other: 13 percent
  • Contracting hospitals: 5 percent

What is the Sandoval County property tax calendar?

The county runs on a tax calendar rather than a regular one. The Treasurer's FAQ lists the dates that matter, and the Assessor's FAQ cites the statutes behind them.

DateWhat happens
January 1Date of assessment; ownership and values are set as of this day
February 28Last day to report value changes, apply for exemptions or remove destroyed property
April 1Assessor mails the Notice of Value
October 1Tax roll goes from the Assessor to the Treasurer
November 1Tax bills mailed; the only bill the owner receives
November 10 to December 10First half due, without penalty through December 10
April 10 to May 10Second half due, without penalty through May 10
June 10Delinquent notices prepared and mailed
July 1Delinquency list for parcels over two years behind goes to the state

Late charges are 1 percent of the base tax per month in interest, plus 1 percent per month in penalty, with a penalty maximum of 5 percent and a minimum of $5. A returned check adds $25 or 5 percent of the check, whichever is greater.

How do Sandoval County owners keep their tax records correct?

Owners keep the record correct by telling the Assessor about changes in writing. The Treasurer's FAQ says any change of address must be submitted in writing and signed by the property owner on record with the Assessor, because bills go to the address on the Assessor's roll and may not be forwarded if more than six months have passed since a move.

The FAQ lists other reasons a bill may not arrive: a change of address received after bills were printed, a data entry error, or mail lost among the more than 100,000 bills the office sends. It also lists why a bill may rise: a higher assessed value, a lost exemption, a different school district, a higher mil levy or a voter-approved bond.

For a seller, a clean record speeds up a closing. Before listing or accepting an offer, confirm the owner of record, the mailing address and the status of both halves of the current year, then ask the Treasurer for a statement of taxes due.

How do I contest a Sandoval County valuation?

The protest window runs thirty days from the date the Notice of Value is mailed. The Assessor's FAQ describes the last day of that thirty-day period as the final date to file a valuation protest, to claim a family or veteran exemption, to apply for agricultural valuation, to report improvements costing more than $10,000 or to submit a statement of decrease in value.

The state's protest pamphlet sets the content of a petition: owner name and address, a property description, the reason the value is wrong and the value the owner believes is correct. A three-member county valuation protests board hears it and must decide within 180 days, and a decision can go to district court within thirty days.

The cap on residential increases also applies here: the higher of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years back. A first-year valuation, new improvements and a change of ownership in the prior year are exceptions.

What happens to the tax bill when a Sandoval County house is sold?

The county does not prorate property tax, and the bill follows the owner on record. The Treasurer's FAQ says taxes cannot be prorated and that a bill goes to every owner even when a mortgage company pays it. Because the division of the year between seller and buyer is not something the county does, it is settled in the sale paperwork instead.

Several practical points follow from that FAQ:

  • If the property is sold after October 1, the bill still carries the previous owner's name and address.
  • New owners should give the Assessor a mailing address as soon as the deed is recorded with the County Clerk.
  • A mobile home needs a tax release before a title transfer, paid in certified funds, and releases are by appointment only.
  • Property tax liability exists even if a bill was never received, under Section 7-38-36 NMSA 1978.

The Treasurer adds that the State of New Mexico and its counties do not run tax deed, tax certificate or tax lien sales. The only sales are state auctions for parcels with two or more years of delinquent tax. Cash Home Buyers works with Sandoval County owners who want to sell before that point, with no repairs and no commission.

Where is the Sandoval County Treasurer's office?

It is at 1500 Idalia Road, Building D, in Bernalillo, NM 87004, on the first floor. Call 505-867-7581 or 1-800-332-8022, or write to P.O. Box 40, Bernalillo, NM 87004.

When are Sandoval County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 and is paid without penalty through December 10. The second half is due April 10 and is paid without penalty through May 10.

What are the late fees on Sandoval County property tax?

Interest is 1 percent of the base tax per month. The penalty is also 1 percent per month, capped at 5 percent, with a $5 minimum.

Will I get a bill if my mortgage company pays my tax?

Yes. Every property owner in Sandoval County is mailed a bill, even when the mortgage company pays it.

Does the county prorate property tax when I sell?

No. The Treasurer states taxes cannot be prorated. Sellers and buyers settle the split in their sale paperwork.

Can Sandoval County sell my house for unpaid tax?

Not the county itself. The state conducts auctions for parcels with two or more years of delinquent property tax, and the Treasurer sends the delinquency list to the state on July 1.

Where is Eddy County, New Mexico, and what is in it?

Eddy County sits in the southeast corner of New Mexico, along the Texas line, and covers 4,198 square miles. Carlsbad is the county seat. Artesia is the other city, and the villages are Hope and Loving.

The county touches Otero County to the west, Chaves County to the north and Lea County to the east, with Loving, Reeves and Culberson counties in Texas to the south and southeast. The lowest point in New Mexico is in Eddy County, at Red Bluff Reservoir, where the Pecos River leaves the state. Carlsbad Caverns National Park is inside the county lines.

The 2020 census counted 62,314 people, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 62,509. The state legislature's official 2020 table splits that population as follows.

Place in Eddy County2020 census population
Carlsbad (county seat)32,238
Artesia12,875
Loving1,390
Rest of the county15,811
Eddy County total62,314

Roughly a quarter of residents live outside any incorporated place, and a house out there is taxed by a different mix of districts than one inside Carlsbad or Artesia.

How did Eddy County get its shape?

Cattle, canals, railroad, oil and potash built Eddy County, in about that order. Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving drove herds along the Pecos in 1866, and Charles B. Eddy arrived in 1881 and later formed the Pecos Valley Land and Ditch Company. The county is named for him.

A town called Eddy was incorporated on September 15, 1888, and the territorial legislature set the county boundaries in 1889. The town changed its name to Carlsbad in 1899. The first Pecos Valley Railroad train arrived on January 10, 1891, which made it easier to move cotton, alfalfa, cattle and settlers.

  • 1902: Carlsbad Caverns were discovered about 18 miles southwest of Carlsbad.
  • 1909: oil was found near Dayton, about 8 miles south of Artesia, and a larger strike followed near Artesia in 1923.
  • 1925: geologist V. H. McNutt found major potash deposits while looking for oil east of Carlsbad.

What drives the Eddy County economy?

Oil and gas, potash, nuclear waste storage, manufacturing and tourism carry most of Eddy County's economy. Carlsbad's economic development office describes potash mining, nuclear storage, oil and gas, and manufacturing as significant pillars, with medical, aviation and tourism adding to them.

The Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, known as WIPP, is a federal site in the county. The Department of Energy's site report places it 26 miles east of Carlsbad on 10,240 acres in the Chihuahuan Desert. The same economic development release said that as of June 2022 Eddy County led the nation with 53 active drilling rigs.

For a seller this matters in two ways. Demand for housing follows the drilling and plant schedules, so it can swing faster than in a county with a steadier employer base. And workers on short assignments often rent, which is why many Eddy County owners end up as landlords. The Census Bureau figures on this page's header put the owner-occupied share at 75 percent.

  • Schools: Artesia Public Schools, Carlsbad Municipal School District and Loving Municipal Schools serve parts of the county.
  • Roads: US 62/180, US 82 and US 285 are the main highways, plus a network of state routes such as NM 31, NM 128 and NM 137.

Who values houses and who collects the tax in Eddy County?

The Eddy County Assessor values property, and the Eddy County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. State law gives the county assessor the job of valuing property in the county, other than railroads, pipelines, utilities, airlines, power plants and mineral property, which the state Taxation and Revenue Department values itself.

That carve-out is large in a place like Eddy County. A 2024 presentation to legislators said the state department assessed 531 properties statewide worth $32 billion, about 17 percent of the tax base.

OfficeRoleContact listed on county pages
Eddy County TreasurerBills and collects property tax101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, Carlsbad, NM 88220; (575) 885-3913
Eddy County AssessorValues property, handles exemptions and protests(575) 885-3813
Online paymentTreasurer bills by searchPoint and Pay portal linked from the county site

Phone numbers and addresses change, so confirm them on the treasurer's page and the assessor's page before you drive over.

When are Eddy County property taxes due?

Eddy County follows the statewide schedule: the first half is due November 10 and the second half is due April 10 of the following year. Bills go out by November 1. You can pay the first half without interest through December 10 and the second half through May 10.

DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for the tax year, and the date the lien attaches
September 1State sets the tax rates
November 1Treasurers mail bills
November 10First installment due
December 10Last day to pay the first half before interest accrues
April 10Second installment due
May 10Last day to pay the second half before interest accrues

Unpaid tax is not a simple debt. State law makes real property taxes a lien from January 1 of the tax year, and it is a first lien, ahead of any other interest in the property, perfected or not. A lien arises without anyone filing a notice, so a recorded-documents search alone will not show it. Ask the treasurer for a current balance before you list or accept an offer.

How is a house valued, and what changes when it sells?

A residential value in Eddy County can rise only 3 percent a year while the same owner holds it, and the cap resets when the property changes hands. The statute says value cannot exceed the higher of 103 percent of the prior year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier. The limit does not apply in the first year a property is valued, to new improvements, after a change of ownership or after a change of use or zoning.

Taxable value is one third of assessed value, and rates are set after yield control adjusts them. Residential property was 49 percent of the statewide net taxable value in tax year 2022. The Tax Foundation puts New Mexico's effective property tax rate at 0.63 percent, which is low nationally.

The practical result for a seller: the buyer's tax bill can be higher than yours, because the buyer's first-year value is reset to current and correct value. If you have owned for decades, expect the new owner to ask about that jump. The $2,000 head of family exemption applies to a resident's primary home and is removed after a change of ownership, so the buyer has to claim it.

  • Transfers to a spouse, or to a child who lives in the home, are among the listed exceptions to "change of ownership."
  • A transfer into a revocable trust for yourself, your spouse or your child is also excepted.
  • A transfer between you and an LLC you own is a change of ownership, according to a New Mexico Court of Appeals decision.

How do I protest an Eddy County valuation?

File a written petition with the county assessor within 30 days of the date the notice of valuation was mailed, or by April 1, whichever is later. An appeal goes to the county valuation protest board, and one member of that board is a state Taxation and Revenue appraiser.

Filing a timely protest keeps the disputed part of the tax from going delinquent. You can instead pay and then file a refund claim in district court; the state's calendar sets January 10 of the following year as the last day for that claim.

The state's protest pamphlet lists the statute citations.

What happens if Eddy County property tax goes unpaid?

Interest starts after the December 10 and May 10 dates, and the account is handed to the state at the end of the third full year of delinquency. The Delinquent Property Tax Bureau then contacts the owner by phone, certified mail, site visits and notices posted on the property. It offers installment agreements and, as a last resort, lists the property for public auction. A state presentation says the law requires an auction in each county every calendar year.

If the property sells at auction, the unpaid tax, penalty, interest and costs come off first, and any remainder goes to the former owner. That is a poor way to exit a house you could have sold.

  • An inherited home may carry bills mailed to the person who died.
  • Absentee owners of rural parcels may miss notices sent to an old address.

What should a seller in Eddy County check before a cash sale?

Start with the treasurer's balance, the assessor's record of who owns the land and the minerals, and the county clerk's recorded documents. In New Mexico, a deed or mortgage that is not recorded does not affect title or rights as against a later purchaser, so recording matters.

Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, ask who pays recording and title costs, and compare the number against your payoff and any tax due.

When is Eddy County property tax due?

The first half is due November 10 and the second half April 10. You can pay the first half without interest through December 10, and the second half through May 10.

Who do I call about my Eddy County property tax bill?

Call the Eddy County Treasurer at (575) 885-3913 for bills and payments. The office is at 101 W. Greene St., Suite 117, in Carlsbad. Call the Assessor at (575) 885-3813 for valuations and exemptions.

How much can my Eddy County home value increase each year?

By state law a residential value cannot rise more than the higher of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years back. The cap resets when ownership changes.

Is there a New Mexico estate or inheritance tax on an Eddy County house?

No. New Mexico's estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005, and the state does not impose an inheritance tax. Federal estate tax can still apply to very large estates.

Can I sell an Eddy County house with property tax owed?

Yes, but the lien runs from January 1 and ranks ahead of other interests, so it has to be paid or settled for the buyer to receive clean title. Get a payoff from the treasurer first.

What is the head of family exemption?

It is a $2,000 reduction in taxable value for a New Mexico resident's primary home. It does not transfer to a buyer automatically, who must claim it after the purchase.

What is Bernalillo County and who runs its property tax?

Bernalillo County is New Mexico's most populous county, with 1,160 square miles and more than 676,000 residents, and two elected officials run its property tax: the Assessor values property and the Treasurer bills and collects. The county government also has five commissioners, a clerk, a probate judge and a sheriff.

A county news release says the government serves residents of Albuquerque, Los Ranchos and Tijeras, and that about 106,000 people live in unincorporated areas. Albuquerque is the county seat. Both offices share Alvarado Square at 415 Silver Ave SW. The Assessor can be reached at (505) 222-3700 and the Treasurer at (505) 468-7031.

The Assessor describes its job as valuing real property, business personal property, livestock and manufactured homes, notifying owners and preparing the tax roll for the Treasurer.

How does the Bernalillo County property tax year work?

Value is fixed on January 1, notices go out by April 1, rates are set in September, the roll goes to the Treasurer by October 1, and bills are mailed by early November. Each step comes from the Assessor's FAQ and the Treasurer's pages.

StepTimingWho
Property valued as of its conditionJanuary 1Assessor
Exemption and Head of Family applicationsLast day of February, or 30 days after the Notice of ValueAssessor
Notices of Value mailedBy April 1Assessor
Assessor certifies valuation to the stateJune 15Assessor
Delinquent notices mailedAbout June 10Treasurer
Rates set by stateSeptemberDept. of Finance and Administration
Tax roll deliveredOctober 1Assessor to Treasurer
Bills mailed, first half dueNovember 1 and November 10Treasurer
Second half dueApril 10Treasurer

The 2026 roll was delivered on October 1, and the Treasurer said bills would be mailed by November 2 because November 1 was a Sunday. Owners who are not on the 10-month payment agreement can pay in full or in two installments.

How are Bernalillo County taxes calculated?

Taxable value is one-third of the assessed value, and the exemption comes off that figure before the mill rate is applied. The Assessor's FAQ defines net taxable value as taxable value minus exemptions such as Head of Family and the veterans' exemption.

The state sets the rates. In an October 2025 post, the Treasurer said the Department of Finance and Administration affirmed 2025 mill rates, that many rates fell compared with 2024, and that rising valuation, a new taxing district and additional tax initiatives would still push bills up across the county. Rates differ by taxing district, so the Assessor's property search and the Treasurer's rate charts for 2016 to 2025 are the right places to find a figure for one address.

New Mexico law caps annual growth in taxable value of residential property at 3%, a rule the Doña Ana County Assessor describes and the Bernalillo County Assessor applies to manufactured homes as well. The cap limits assessment growth, not the mill rate.

What tax savings programs does Bernalillo County offer?

The Assessor lists Head of Family, veteran and disabled veteran exemptions and a value freeze. A separate protest form is not needed for any of them.

  • Head of Family takes $2,000 off taxable value for one property per household in the state.
  • The veteran exemption takes up to $10,000 off taxable value with a certificate from the New Mexico Veterans' Service Commission. Once granted, it stays on the record.
  • Disabled veterans can exempt a percentage of the primary residence based on their VA disability rating.
  • The value freeze is for owners 65 or older with modified gross income of $42,900 or less, or disabled owners at $41,900 or less. It stops the assessed value from rising 3% and does not freeze the tax rate.

The deadline for the current year is 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed. The Assessor's tax savings page has the forms. The FAQ also notes that a value freeze does not force you to sell at the frozen value.

How do I appeal a Bernalillo County valuation?

File a protest with the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing, online through the appeal portal or at 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal meeting with a field appraiser follows, and a hearing before the Protest Valuation Review Board comes next if the value is not resolved.

For the 2026 tax year, business personal property, manufactured home and livestock protests ran from May 1 to a June 1 deadline. An owner who received an amended Notice of Value gets 30 days from the amended mailing date.

Someone who misses the window can still pay the bill and file a claim for refund in the Second Judicial District Court at 400 Lomas Blvd NW. The Treasurer says the claim must be filed by the 60th day after the first installment due date and that the bill must be paid first. The court filing fee listed by the Assessor is $132. The Assessor's protest page also gives a January 10 date, so confirm the cutoff with the court self-help center at 505-841-6702 before relying on either.

If a protest is still pending in December, the Treasurer recommends paying the first half on the original bill. A new bill and a refund follow if the protest succeeds, and paying avoids late fees if it does not.

What happens when Bernalillo County property tax is paid late?

Late fees are interest of 1% per month plus a penalty of 1% per month, with the penalty capped at 5% and a minimum of $5. They start December 10 for the first half and May 10 for the second.

The Treasurer accepts payment in person on the first floor of 415 Silver Ave SW, online through the county's payment vendor, or by mail to PO Box 27800, Albuquerque, NM 87125-7800. The office warns against using a bank's bill-pay service, citing mailing delays, misrouting and lack of confirmation. It also says owners are liable even if a bill never arrives, and that roughly 10,600 bills were returned in the 2025 cycle, mostly for outdated addresses.

As of June 2026 the office reported about $917.5 million collected and a rate of nearly 95%. Delinquent notices began mailing June 10.

What should a seller in Bernalillo County know about tax at closing?

The owner of record on January 1 is liable for that year's tax, and a manufactured home needs a tax release before it can be sold, moved or traded. Title companies pull the balance and pay it from the sale proceeds.

The Assessor's FAQ says a manufactured home owner must obtain a tax release from the Treasurer showing current and prior years are paid, and begins that process at the Assessor with proof of ownership. Land and a manufactured home on it get separate notices and bills unless the home has been converted to real property. Public improvement district charges transfer to the buyer, and a seller can prepay the balance.

After closing, file the residential transfer affidavit with the Assessor within 30 days, as covered in our Bernalillo County Clerk guide. Sellers carrying back taxes, an inherited house or a tenant-occupied property often sell as-is for cash to avoid repairs and showings, and the tax balance comes out of the proceeds either way.

More questions about Bernalillo County, NM Property Tax Guide

When are Bernalillo County property taxes due?

The first half is due November 10 and the second half April 10. Late fees begin December 10 and May 10, according to the Bernalillo County Treasurer.

Who sets property values in Bernalillo County?

The elected County Assessor sets values and mails Notices of Value by April 1. The elected Treasurer bills and collects the tax, and the state sets mill rates each September.

How do I protest my Bernalillo County valuation?

File a protest form with the Assessor within 30 days of the Notice of Value mailing, online or at 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal meeting and, if needed, a Protest Valuation Review Board hearing follow.

What exemptions can Bernalillo County homeowners claim?

Head of Family reduces taxable value by $2,000, veterans can claim up to $10,000, disabled veterans can exempt a percentage of their primary residence, and eligible seniors or disabled owners can apply for a value freeze.

Can I sell a Bernalillo County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The title company normally pays the balance, including penalty and interest, from the sale proceeds at closing. Confirm the figure with the Treasurer at (505) 468-7031.

Does Bernalillo County send a bill if a mortgage company pays my taxes?

Yes. Every owner receives a bill even when a lender pays. The bill lists the mortgage company that requested the amount, and the owner stays responsible for making sure it is paid.

What is San Juan County, NM, and where does it sit?

San Juan County fills the northwest corner of New Mexico and includes the state's portion of the Four Corners. According to Wikipedia, it was created in 1887, its county seat is Aztec, and its 2020 census population of 121,661 made it the fifth-most populous county in the state. It is part of the Farmington metropolitan statistical area.

The county covers 5,538 square miles, and the San Juan, Animas and La Plata rivers cross it. The Navajo Nation takes up 60.45 percent of the county's area, so a large part of the county sits outside the ordinary city lots of Farmington, Aztec and Bloomfield.

Communities named on the same page include Farmington, Aztec, Bloomfield and Kirtland, plus Flora Vista, Fruitland, Waterflow, Shiprock, Lee Acres, Navajo Dam and Nenahnezad. Rates reflect the school district, city and voter-approved bonds that cover a given property, so the location of a house affects its bill.

Who are the major employers in San Juan County?

Energy, health care and education lead the list. Four Corners Economic Development names San Juan Regional Medical Center, Farmington Municipal Schools, San Juan College, the City of Farmington and San Juan County itself among the major employers. It also lists Hilcorp, Enterprise Products Partners, Arizona Public Service, Public Service Company of New Mexico, Indian Health Services, the Navajo Agricultural Products Industry and the Northern Edge Navajo Casino.

The same organization's talent page puts county employment at roughly 48,000 workers, with health care the largest sector at 17 percent and retail at 12 percent.

  • Health care: San Juan Regional Medical Center, Indian Health Services, Presbyterian Medical Services
  • Education: Farmington Municipal Schools, San Juan College
  • Energy and utilities: Hilcorp, Enterprise Products Partners, Arizona Public Service, PNM
  • Agriculture and gaming: Navajo Agricultural Products Industry, Northern Edge Navajo Casino

How are San Juan County property taxes calculated?

The taxable value is one third of the full value, and the rate is applied to that amount. The San Juan County Assessor's FAQ explains that the Assessor compiles a tax roll, a county appraiser sets the full value, and the tax rate is stated in dollars per thousand.

The rate comes from outside the county offices. The Assessor's page says the State Department of Finance and Administration sets it every year from budgets submitted by schools, cities and voters through approved bond issues, and certifies it each September. Valuation changes are usually caused by additions to a building or by the reappraisal the Legislature requires every two years.

A worked example makes the structure clear without promising any figure. If an appraiser set a full value of $300,000, the taxable value would be $100,000, and the rate in dollars per thousand would apply to that $100,000, before any exemption.

When are San Juan County property taxes due, and what happens when they are late?

The first half and the full year are due on November 10, and the second half is due on April 10. The Treasurer's notifications page says bills are released on November 1, penalty and interest begin December 11 on the first half, and begin May 11 on the second half.

The Treasurer sends a reminder notice on April 1 to owners with a balance from earlier years, and a delinquent notice after the second-half due date. The page warns that three or more years of back taxes can put a property on the State of New Mexico's auction list.

Payment can be made five ways:

  • In person at the Treasurer's windows, 100 S. Oliver Dr., Suite 300, Aztec, NM 87410
  • By mail to the processing center at San Juan County Treasurer Dept. #31087, P.O. Box 27839, Albuquerque, NM 87125-7839
  • By mail to the physical address in Aztec
  • In the drop box on the east side of the County Administration building
  • Online through the county's tax portal

The Treasurer also notes that a valid mailing address is needed for timely delivery, and the Assessor at 505-334-6157 handles address changes. The Assessor adds that not getting a bill does not remove the duty to pay, including late charges.

What exemptions and limits can lower a San Juan County bill?

Three programs come up most often: the head of family exemption, the veteran exemption and the valuation freeze for some older or disabled owners. The Assessor says the head of family exemption is $2,000, deducted from taxable value, applies to residential property only, and renews automatically once claimed.

The veteran exemption requires an honorably discharged veteran living in New Mexico to present a certificate of eligibility from the Veterans Service Office to the Assessor in person between January 1 and April 30. A disabled veteran's occupied principal residence can be exempt in an amount equal to the federal disability percentage. The county lists the Veterans Service Office at 1800 E. 30th St., Farmington.

The limitation on increase in value applies to a single-family dwelling owned and occupied by a person aged 65 or older, or disabled, whose income stays under an inflation-adjusted limit. The county says the owner must apply, and apply again each year for three years.

Separately, state law caps residential value growth. Under Section 7-36-21.2, as shown in the state's protest pamphlet, the value may not exceed the higher of 103 percent of the prior year or 106.1 percent of two years earlier. A change of ownership in the prior year lifts that cap for the following tax year.

How do I protest a San Juan County valuation?

Visit the Assessor first, then file a protest if the appraiser cannot resolve it. The county's FAQ says to talk to an appraiser in person, and if you still disagree, request a protest packet. You have thirty days from the mailing date of the Notice of Value to file with the County Valuation Protest Board through the Assessor's office.

The Assessor notifies the owner by certified mail at least fifteen days before the hearing, and the FAQ states plainly that state law puts the burden of proving the value wrong on the owner. Bring evidence: recent comparable sales, a repair estimate, photographs of damage or a recent appraisal.

An owner who files nothing should not read much into a notice. The Assessor's page says a Notice of Value is not a tax bill, and that if the value, mailing address and property description are right, no action is needed.

What should a San Juan County owner know before selling?

The main points are the mobile home release, the flood notice on the county's website and the state auction rule. A mobile home tax release is required for a duplicate title, a title change and a moving permit, and the Treasurer charges $5 for a regular release and $25 for a moving permit. Payment for those transactions is by certified funds only, and the county does not take personal or business checks.

Unpaid mobile home and personal property tax follows its own collection path. The Treasurer says a Pre-Demand Warrant gives ten business days to pay or arrange payment, after which a Demand Warrant is served by a deputy sheriff with a $42 fee for each delivery.

At the time of writing, the county's website carries a banner describing catastrophic flooding along the San Juan and Animas rivers. Owners near those rivers who sell should keep damage records and insurance claim papers together, since both affect what a buyer will pay.

For real estate, the State Property Tax Division holds the auction of long-delinquent parcels, sells them as is, and sells with no right of redemption. Cash Home Buyers speaks with San Juan County owners who would rather close on their own timeline than wait for that.

The first half and full amount are due November 10, and the second half is due April 10. Penalty and interest start December 11 on the first half and May 11 on the second.

Where do I pay San Juan County property tax?

The Treasurer's office is at 100 S. Oliver Dr., Suite 300, in Aztec. You can also pay by mail, at the drop box on the east side of the administration building, or online through the county's portal.

What is taxable value in San Juan County?

Taxable value is one third of the full value set by the county appraiser. The tax rate, in dollars per thousand, is applied to that taxable value.

You have thirty days from the date the Notice of Value was mailed. File through the Assessor's office with the County Valuation Protest Board; the owner carries the burden of showing the value is wrong.

It is $2,000, deducted from taxable value on residential property only. After you sign up, it renews automatically each year.

What happens after three years of unpaid property tax in San Juan County?

The property can be added to the auction list kept by the State of New Mexico. The Treasurer's notices say failure to pay three or more years of back taxes could lead to that.

Where is Doña Ana County and what is in it?

Doña Ana County is the second largest county in New Mexico, covering 3,814 square miles along the Texas and Mexico borders in the south of the state. The county reports more than 219,500 residents.

Its own About Us page lists the neighbors: El Paso County in Texas, Luna and Otero Counties in New Mexico, and the Mexican state of Chihuahua. The county contains the cities of Anthony, Las Cruces and Sunland Park, the Town of Mesilla and the Village of Hatch. Agriculture is a major industry, with the county naming itself a leading producer of chile peppers, onions and pecans. New Mexico State University and Doña Ana Community College are based here, and the Organ Mountains Desert Peaks and White Sands national monuments are among its landmarks.

For a seller, that mix means very different property types under one tax office: city lots in Las Cruces, irrigated farm parcels in the Mesilla Valley and open desert acreage.

What is Las Cruces, and how does it shape the county?

Las Cruces is the county seat and the largest city in southern New Mexico. According to Wikipedia's Las Cruces entry, it had 111,385 residents in the 2020 census, which made it the second most populous city in the state, and it sits at an elevation near 3,900 feet.

The city is the center of the Mesilla Valley, the farming region on the Rio Grande floodplain, with the Organ Mountains about 10 miles to the east. The same source names the federal government at White Sands Test Facility and White Sands Missile Range as its major employer, and notes that Spaceport America has corporate offices in the city. New Mexico State University is the state's only land-grant university.

The county's own tax example uses a Las Cruces home, which is a reminder that tax rates vary with the taxing districts a parcel sits in, such as the city, the school district and special districts.

Who handles Doña Ana County property tax?

The Doña Ana County Assessor values property, and the Doña Ana County Treasurer bills and collects. The Assessor, Eugenia "Gina" Montoya Ortega, was elected in November 2022 and took office on January 1, 2023.

The Assessor's page puts the split simply: its office does valuation, not taxation. The state Department of Finance and Administration sets the rate each taxing entity receives, called the mill levy. Cities, school districts and other entities take a share based on their budgets.

The Treasurer's property tax FAQ gives the formula: taxable value minus exemptions, multiplied by the mill rate, equals taxes due. Its sample uses a $100,000 Las Cruces home. One-third is $33,333.33 in taxable value, the $2,000 head of household deduction brings it to $31,333.33, and a mill levy rate of 0.029269 yields $917.10. That is the county's illustration, so check your own district's rate on the Assessor's site.

What are the Doña Ana County tax dates?

First-half tax is due November 10 and becomes delinquent after December 10. Second-half tax is due April 10 and becomes delinquent after May 10. This is the county Treasurer's calendar.

Some social media posts from the county speak of taxes being "due" by December 10, which can read as a conflict. The Treasurer's FAQ is the better reference: November 10 is the due date and December 10 is the last day before delinquency charges apply on December 11.

What does late payment cost in Doña Ana County?

Interest accrues at 1% of the base tax each month until paid, and a 1% penalty accrues for up to five months, with a $5 minimum penalty. A returned check carries a $25 fee.

The Treasurer says no law lets a county treasurer waive penalty or interest, and that no other body, including the Governor, can remove them once accrued. A missing bill is not a defense, because owners must pay on time whether or not a bill arrived.

The consequences escalate over time:

  • Each June the Treasurer mails a notice for any bill 30 or more days delinquent.
  • Delinquent taxes are transferred to the state's Property Tax Division on July 1.
  • Real property with taxes unpaid for two years from the delinquency date can be sold at state public auction.
  • Owners of three or more years of prior taxes have the property sold unless all years are paid in full by the sale date.
  • Manufactured homes and personal property can be seized and sold after six months.

An owner who cannot pay in full can ask the state Property Tax Division about an installment agreement to stop a sale.

How can a Doña Ana County homeowner protest or reduce the bill?

File a valuation protest with the County Assessor within 30 days of the date on the Notice of Value, usually during April. If you miss it, pay the full bill by December 10 and file a claim for refund in District Court by January 10.

A pending protest does not suspend payment. You must pay at least the tax on the value not in dispute by December 10, and by May 10 for the second half. If a protest results in a corrected bill, it carries a new delinquency date and arrives at least 30 days before payment is due, without interest or penalty on the amended amount.

Under the FAQ, New Mexico has no homestead exemption. The relief available is:

  • Head of Family, for a resident whose primary residence it is. You apply once and it continues, one per household.
  • A veteran exemption, which requires a certificate from the New Mexico Veterans' Service Commission taken to the Assessor during the Notice of Value period.
  • A valuation freeze for owners 65 or older or disabled, with modified gross income under $35,000, applied for in three consecutive years before it stays in place while you live there.

Those freeze terms come from the Doña Ana FAQ and differ from the figures Bernalillo County publishes, so confirm current limits with the Assessor.

What matters when selling a Doña Ana County house with tax due?

The owner of record on January 1 is responsible for that year's tax, and a tax lien stays on the property regardless of later ownership changes. The Treasurer cites section 7-37-7 NMSA 1978 for this rule.

The Treasurer also answers the proration question directly: taxes cannot be prorated by the county. Any split between buyer and seller is a matter for the sale contract and the closing statement, which a title company prepares. If the property is mortgaged, the owner must make sure the lender has paid, and the county does not mail an escrowed bill to the owner, though you can request one.

Special situations to watch:

  • A mobile home needs a property tax release from the Assessor before its title can transfer or a moving permit issue, and personal checks are not accepted for the release payment.
  • A land split or combination requires taxes paid in full, including the current year, before the Treasurer issues a Certification of Taxes Paid.
  • A closed business still owes tax for the year if it operated on January 1.

Sellers with farm parcels, inherited land or several years of back tax often choose an as-is cash sale, and the title company pays what is owed from the proceeds.

The first half is due November 10 and becomes delinquent after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and becomes delinquent after May 10, per the county Treasurer.

Interest is 1% of the base tax per month, and a 1% penalty accrues for up to five months, with a $5 minimum. The Treasurer says these cannot be waived.

Can Doña Ana County property taxes be prorated?

No, the county Treasurer states that taxes cannot be prorated. Buyers and sellers divide the tax in their contract and at closing.

How long do I have to protest my Doña Ana County valuation?

You have 30 days from the date of the Notice of Value, usually in April. A later claim for refund requires paying the full bill and filing in District Court by January 10.

What happens if I do not pay Doña Ana County property tax?

Delinquent taxes move to the state Property Tax Division on July 1. Real property can be sold at state auction when taxes stay unpaid for two years, or sooner when three or more years are owed.

No. New Mexico has Head of Family and veteran exemptions instead, plus a valuation freeze for qualifying older or disabled owners.

Where is Socorro County and what is in it?

Socorro County is a large, thinly settled county in central New Mexico, with Socorro as its county seat. It was formed in 1852 and covers about 6,649 square miles, and the 2020 census counted 16,595 residents.

The county borders Cibola, Valencia, Torrance, Lincoln, Sierra and Catron counties. Interstate 25, U.S. 60 and U.S. 380 cross it. Its communities include Socorro, Magdalena, San Antonio, Lemitar, Polvadera and Veguita. Features in or near the county include the Rio Grande, Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, the Very Large Array, the Trinity Site, New Mexico Tech and part of the Cibola National Forest.

For property tax, size matters. A parcel can be a lot in the city of Socorro, a small property along the river valley, or acreage far from a town, and the assessor values each by its own type and use.

New Mexico Tech was founded in 1889 as the New Mexico School of Mines.

With a county population of about 16,600 spread over thousands of square miles, a rural or vacant parcel may take longer to find a buyer than a house in the city of Socorro.

Which offices handle property tax in Socorro County?

Two elected offices handle property tax in Socorro County: the Assessor sets values and the Treasurer collects the money.

  • Assessor: PO Box J, 200 Church St, Socorro, NM 87801. Phone 575-835-0714. The office values homes, businesses and other taxable property and prepares the tax rolls for the Treasurer.
  • Treasurer: PO Box KK, 200 Church St, Socorro, NM 87801. Phone 575-835-1701. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the office is closed on federal holidays.
  • State Property Tax Division: Manuel Lujan Building, 1200 S. St. Francis Drive, Santa Fe, which takes over accounts that stay delinquent.

The county says it does not sell or broker real property and does not give advice on real property transactions, so use a title company or attorney for closing questions.

How is Socorro County property valued and how can you appeal?

The assessor mails Notices of Valuation to all owners by April 1, and the notice shows the value used to compute the tax. Taxable value is one-third of the appraised value, minus any allowable exemptions such as head of household or veteran exemptions.

An owner may protest the assessor's value or classification, the allocation of value to a taxing unit, a denial of an exemption, or a limit on a value increase. Under Section 7-38-24, as quoted in 2026 House Bill 285, the petition is filed with the county assessor, generally within 30 days after the notice is mailed. Where the notice was mailed with the prior year's tax bill, the deadline is the later of April 1 or 30 days after mailing.

HB 285 also amended the disabled veteran exemption. It sets the exemption at the veteran's federal disability percentage times taxable value, provided the veteran lives in the home as a principal residence. It also lets a veteran who sells or transfers a principal residence keep the exemption for the rest of the year or move it to a new home.

You can pay in person, by phone at 575-835-1701, online with a card or e-check, or by mail to PO Box KK. The Treasurer warns never to mail cash. If you have not received a bill by November 15, call 575-835-0714, because state law makes the owner responsible even without a bill.

What happens if you sell a Socorro County property with tax still due?

Unpaid property tax does not disappear when a house is sold, so the closing needs to account for it. New Mexico taxes are a lien from January 1 of the tax year, as other county assessors in the state explain, and the title company will look for open balances.

The delinquency path is set by state law, and Socorro County's Treasurer describes it this way:

  • Owners of three or more years of back taxes will have the property sold by the State unless all years are paid before the sale.
  • An owner who cannot pay in full can ask the State Property Tax Division for an installment agreement to stop a sale.

The county posted a notice for a public auction on October 1, 2024, at 10:00 a.m. at 200 Church St in Socorro. The State publishes the sale lists in a newspaper for three weeks before each sale.

  • Cash offer: from a buyer who purchases as-is, which can help when taxes are behind or the home is in a remote location. Ask for the offer in writing.

If you inherited property in Socorro County, the Assessor's records follow recorded documents, so deeds and death certificates must be recorded with the county clerk before ownership shows up on the tax roll. Where is Otero County, New Mexico, and how is it laid out?

The county was founded on January 30, 1899, and is named for Miguel Antonio Otero, the territorial governor at the time.

The people are concentrated in a few places. Alamogordo is the only city. Cloudcroft and Tularosa are villages, and the census lists a long run of smaller places: Boles Acres, High Rolls, La Luz, Mayhill, Mescalero, Orogrande, Timberon and Holloman AFB, among others. The Mescalero Apache Indian Reservation and part of Lincoln National Forest take up other ground, and part of White Sands National Park lies inside the county line.

The same entry notes that the western part of the county was handed to the Army as the country prepared to enter World War II and later became part of White Sands Missile Range.

What drives the Otero County economy?

Holloman Air Force Base is the largest employer in the area, according to the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce. The chamber says the base is home to the 49th Wing, which trains F-16 and MQ-9 pilots, and to the 46th Test Group, which tests radars and weapons systems on a high-speed track.

Tourism comes second in the chamber's account. It names the Lodge in Cloudcroft and the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and Casino as flagships that together employ more than 1,000 hospitality workers, and it describes White Sands National Park as drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors a year. Gerald Champion Regional Medical Center, which the chamber calls a joint venture with Holloman, anchors health care.

For a seller, this mix has a practical meaning. Some owners are posted to the base for a set tour and leave on a fixed date, which can leave little time to manage repairs, a tax bill or a listing.

  • Military employment: Holloman AFB, the area's largest employer
  • Hospitality: the Cloudcroft lodge and the Mescalero casino resort
  • Health care: Gerald Champion Regional Medical Center
  • Visitor traffic: White Sands National Park

Which Otero County offices handle property tax?

Two county offices share the work, and both sit at the same Alamogordo address. The Assessor finds, lists and values property. The Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. If you disagree with a value you talk to the Assessor; if you want a payoff figure you ask the Treasurer.

Otero County TreasurerBills and collects property tax, takes payments1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310; 575-437-2030
NM Property Tax DivisionRuns auctions of property with long-delinquent taxSanta Fe; 505-827-0883

Both county offices publish searchable records online through the Treasurer's EagleWeb portal and the Assessor's portal. The assessor portal says it lets you look up current ownership, and the treasurer portal is where a balance can be checked before a sale.

When are Otero County property taxes due?

Taxes are due in two installments. The Otero County Treasurer's page says the first half is due November 10, and other New Mexico county treasurers, such as Sandoval and San Juan, publish the usual statewide pattern: the first half is delinquent after December 10, the second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10.

The Treasurer takes payment in person, by mail, online and by phone. The county's pay-by-phone page gives 1-877-707-1126, or 575-437-2030 and option 2, and lists the card fees: 2.39 percent with a $1.95 minimum on a credit card and $3.95 on a debit card.

  • November 10: first half due
  • December 10: last day for the first half without penalty
  • April 10: second half due
  • May 10: last day for the second half without penalty

A bill that is not received is still owed. New Mexico is a self-rendering state, and the county's duty to mail a bill does not erase the owner's duty to pay.

How does Otero County value a home, and can the value be protested?

The Assessor sets the value, and the owner has 30 days to protest it. Under Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978, as reproduced in the state's protest pamphlet, a petition is filed with the county assessor by the later of April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. It must name the owner and property, say why the value is wrong, and state what the owner believes the correct value is.

Each county has a valuation protests board of three voting members, and the pamphlet says protests must be decided within 180 days of filing. A disagreement with the board can go to district court within thirty days of the board's order.

Home values for tax purposes are also capped. Section 7-36-21.2 limits the value of a residential property to the higher of 103 percent of the prior year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier. The cap does not apply in the first year a property is valued, to improvements made in the prior year, or in a year after a change of ownership or a change of use or zoning.

That last exception matters to anyone planning a sale. A buyer can see a higher assessed value the year after closing, so the seller's old bill is a poor guide to what the new owner will pay.

What happens if property tax goes unpaid on an Otero County house?

Unpaid tax first brings penalty and interest, and after enough years it can lead to a state auction. The Taxation and Revenue Department's auction page says the Property Tax Division, not the county, holds these sales, that the minimum bid is based on taxes, penalty, interest and costs, and that sales are held where title research is done and other collection steps are exhausted. The division does not hold sales in all 33 counties each year.

The page also spells out what a tax sale does and does not clear. A sale extinguishes the tax lien only; no other liens are extinguished. The state issues a tax deed that works like a quitclaim deed and does not warrant title. New Mexico has no right of redemption for former owners, though the page describes a two-year window to challenge the sale in court under Section 7-38-70.

If you own an Otero County house with several years of tax behind it, that clock is the reason to act early. Selling before the property reaches an auction list keeps the equity with you.

What do Otero County sellers with tax due usually need to sort out?

Most sellers need three things done: a current payoff figure, a clean record of who owns the property, and a plan for the two installments. The Treasurer can supply the balance, and the title or escrow company will ask for it before closing.

  • Check the balance on the Treasurer's portal and confirm both halves of the current year.
  • Look for older years. Back tax that has been delinquent for years is the amount that can move a property toward auction.
  • Make sure the mailing address on file is current, because the notice of value and bill go to the address on the tax roll.
  • If the house is a mobile home, ask the Assessor about a tax release, since San Juan and Sandoval counties require one before a mobile home title transfer.

Who is the county seat of Otero County, NM, and where do I pay property tax?

Alamogordo is the county seat. The Otero County Treasurer is at 1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310, phone 575-437-2030, and payments can also be made online or by phone at 1-877-707-1126.

When is the first half of Otero County property tax due?

The first half is due November 10. New Mexico counties treat it as delinquent after December 10, and the second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10.

How long do I have to protest my Otero County valuation?

You have until the later of April 1 or thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. File the petition with the Otero County Assessor, and state why you think the value is wrong and what you believe it should be.

Is there a cap on how fast my home's taxable value can rise?

Yes, for residential property. The value may not exceed the higher of 103 percent of the prior year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier, with exceptions for a first-year valuation, new improvements, a change of ownership and a change of use or zoning.

Can the county sell my house at auction for unpaid tax?

The state, not the county, auctions property after long delinquency. The Property Tax Division sells it as is for at least the taxes, penalty, interest and costs, issues a tax deed without a title warranty, and New Mexico offers no right of redemption.

Can I sell an Otero County house that has tax due?

Yes. The balance is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and a title company will request a payoff figure from the Treasurer. Selling before the property reaches an auction list avoids that outcome.

What and where is San Miguel County, NM?

San Miguel County is a long, narrow county in northeastern New Mexico that runs from the Great Plains to the Rocky Mountains. Wikipedia gives a 2020 census population of 27,201, names Las Vegas as the county seat, and says the county is more than 100 miles long from east to west and 40 miles wide north to south.

The terrain swings a lot. The highest point is Elk Mountain at 11,661 feet, and the lowest is on the Canadian River at about 3,800 feet. The county covers 4,736 square miles, nearly all of it land.

The same entry says the county was created in 1846 by the United States Army during the Mexican-American War. The Santa Fe Trail, first travelled in 1821, passed through it, and the railroad arrived in 1879, which expanded the market for ranch land and the livestock industry, especially sheep for wool.

What towns and communities make up San Miguel County?

Las Vegas is the only city, and the county also has the villages of Pecos and part of Mosquero. The census-designated places include Conchas Dam, East Pecos, Pueblo, Ribera, Rowe, San Jose, Sena, Tecolote, Tecolotito and Villanueva, and smaller communities include Sapello, Rociada, Montezuma, Ilfeld, San Miguel del Vado and Tererro.

Most of these places are small and spread across a county that is 4,736 square miles. A house in Sapello or Rociada is a long way from the services in Las Vegas, so a seller there should expect a buyer to ask about access, utilities and the property's boundaries before agreeing to a price.

Education and public institutions anchor the local economy, and the county's history of ranching and rail still shows. New Mexico Highlands University is listed among the county's higher education institutions on Wikipedia, and United World College, USA occupies the historic Montezuma Castle site northwest of Las Vegas, about 70 miles from Santa Fe, and was founded in 1982.

No official county economic profile with employer counts turned up in our research, so this page makes no claim about the largest employer or job totals. The county entry does say San Miguel County makes up the Las Vegas Micropolitan Statistical Area, which belongs to the larger Albuquerque, Santa Fe and Las Vegas combined statistical area.

If your name or a relative's is on the sale list, the sale lists are also available from the County Treasurer or Assessor. File a written protest with the Assessor within the statutory window. It must give the owner's name and address, describe the property, and explain why the value is wrong and what the correct one is.

The County Assessor's page offers a 2026 protest petition and a 2026 protest pamphlet in English and Spanish. The Assessor's staff is also conducting reappraisals across the county, and the page says appraisers carry county identification and wear safety vests, so a visit from an appraiser is not unusual.

A county valuation protests board of three decides each protest within 180 days, and a decision can be appealed to district court within thirty days. Residential value growth is also limited to the higher of 103 percent of the prior year or 106.1 percent of two years earlier, except after a change of ownership or new improvements.

Where is McKinley County, New Mexico, and who lives there?

McKinley County is in northwest New Mexico on the Arizona line, and Gallup is both its county seat and its only incorporated city. The county covers 5,455 square miles, bordered by San Juan, Sandoval and Cibola counties and by Apache County, Arizona.

The state labor department describes the county as overlapping the Navajo Nation and the Zuni Reservation, with over 60 percent of the land in those two reservation areas. Its 2021 estimate put the population at 75.5 percent American Indian and Alaska Native. The 2020 census counted 72,902 residents, down from 74,798 in 2000, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 68,119.

Land and water area5,455 square miles
2020 census population72,902
Gallup, 202021,899

Population outside those two places, 202048,103

Most residents therefore live outside Gallup, in census-designated places such as Thoreau, Tohatchi, Church Rock, Ramah, Pinehaven and Zuni Pueblo. The Census Bureau lists 44 such places in the county, so the first step for any property here is pinning down exactly which jurisdiction it sits in.

Why does land ownership matter when selling a McKinley County house?

It decides which rules apply, because land inside the reservations is not all taxed or transferred the way private land is. The Bureau of Indian Affairs states that trust land is not subject to state or local taxes, although tribes may tax it to support their own services.

The Navajo Nation Tax Commission separately describes a possessory interest tax, a tax on the right to be on Navajo land for a particular activity such as an oil and gas lease, a right-of-way or a business site lease. Fee land, meaning ordinary privately owned land with a deed, stays under county rules.

  • Fee land with a recorded deed is assessed by the McKinley County Assessor and billed by the Treasurer.
  • Trust land and tribal land assignments follow tribal and federal procedures.
  • Before you price or advertise, confirm whether your land is fee, trust, or held by lease or assignment.

The assessor's records and the county clerk's recorded documents are the quickest way to tell fee land from other holdings. A title company will ask the same question first.

What does the McKinley County economy rest on?

Schools, health care, travel and tribal government do much of the work, and Gallup's position on Interstate 40 feeds a travel trade. The state labor department lists Gallup-McKinley County Schools, Gallup Indian Medical Center and Rehoboth McKinley Christian Health Care Services among the large employers.

Local attractions it names include Fort Wingate, the Gallup Cultural Center, Red Rock State Park and the Inter-Tribal Indian Ceremonial. Part of Chaco Culture National Historical Park and part of the Cibola National Forest lie inside the county. Highways include I-40, with a business loop through Gallup, and US 491.

Water has been a long-running constraint. The Bureau of Reclamation's Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project is designed to carry municipal and industrial water from the San Juan River to the eastern Navajo Nation, part of the Jicarilla Apache Nation and Gallup.

Schools: Gallup-McKinley County Schools run most public schools, among them Gallup High, Miyamura High, Crownpoint High, Thoreau High and Tohatchi High. The Zuni Public School District serves the Zuni area, and the Bureau of Indian Education operates schools near Fort Wingate and in Pueblo Pintado.

Which McKinley County offices handle property tax?

The McKinley County Assessor lists and values taxable property, and the McKinley County Treasurer collects. The treasurer's page says the office collects taxes, penalties and interest under the Property Tax Code, Sections 7-35-1 through 7-38-90 NMSA 1978.

OfficeWhat it doesContact on county pages
County TreasurerCollects property tax, manages county funds207 W Hill Ave, Suite 101, Gallup, NM 87301; (505) 722-4459; 8 AM to 5 PM, Monday to Friday
County AssessorDiscovers, lists and inventories taxable propertyCounty site assessor page
Treasurer online searchLook up an account by property tax account numberTreasurer web portal

The county also publishes charts of taxes billed by taxing entity for each tax year, which show how a bill divides among county, school and other districts. Those charts show amounts billed, not amounts collected. Start at the treasurer's page and the assessor's page.

What are the McKinley County property tax deadlines?

McKinley County uses the state calendar, with payments due November 10 and April 10. A New Mexico Taxation and Revenue schedule sets these steps for every county.

  • January 1: property is valued as of this date, and the tax lien attaches.
  • September 1: the state Department of Finance and Administration sets rates.
  • November 1: treasurers send bills.
  • November 10 and December 10: the first half is due, and interest starts after December 10.
  • April 10 and May 10: the second half is due, and interest starts after May 10.
  • January 10 of the following year: last day to file a refund claim in district court.

Interest on late payments runs at 1 percent a month, according to the scorecard the state department presented to legislators. Because the lien is a first lien under Section 7-38-48, ahead of any other interest, an unpaid McKinley County bill follows the house to whoever owns it next.

How is a McKinley County house valued for tax?

The assessor values it at current and correct value as of January 1, then applies the residential cap. Taxable value is one third of that figure. Residential assessments cannot rise more than 3 percent a year unless the property changes ownership, is improved or is rezoned.

The Census Bureau figures on this page's header show a median home value of $72,100 in McKinley County, well below the state midpoint. Lower values mean smaller absolute bills, but the rules do not change: a late payment still draws interest, and a delinquent account still ends up at the state.

Two details matter in a sale. A change of ownership removes the cap, so the buyer's first valuation is a fresh one. And the $2,000 head of family exemption belongs to a resident's primary home and is removed when ownership changes. A transfer to a child who occupies the home as a principal residence, or into a revocable trust for the owner's spouse or child, is excluded from the definition of change of ownership.

What can a McKinley County owner do about a high valuation?

File a written petition with the assessor within 30 days of the mailing of the notice of valuation, or by April 1, whichever is later. Protests go to a county valuation protest board, which includes one member from the state's Appraisal Bureau.

A timely protest keeps the disputed part of the tax from becoming delinquent. The other route is to pay first and file a refund claim in district court. The scorecard in the state's 2024 legislative presentation shows no fee for an initial protest, and the department publishes a protest pamphlet.

What happens to unpaid McKinley County property tax?

After three full years of delinquency, the account moves to the state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau, which can sell the property at public auction. Before that, the bureau tries phone calls, certified mail, site visits and notices left on the property, and it offers installment agreements.

If an auction sale brings more than the tax, penalty, interest and costs, the remainder goes to the former owner. State law requires an auction in each county every year, so McKinley County is not an exception.

  • Heirs who inherit a house on fee land should check the treasurer's account before listing.
  • Owners who moved away should confirm the treasurer has a current mailing address.

How does a quick sale usually work in McKinley County?

The seller proves ownership, clears any tax lien, and signs a deed that is recorded with the county clerk. Under Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978, an unrecorded deed does not affect title against a later purchaser, so recording protects the buyer.

If a house has an estate attached, the probate steps come first. New Mexico's court self-help guide says an estate with real property cannot use the small-estate affidavit, and a personal representative's deed may be needed to move title out of the decedent's name.

Who collects property tax in McKinley County, NM?

The McKinley County Treasurer, at 207 W Hill Ave, Suite 101, in Gallup, phone (505) 722-4459. The office is open 8 AM to 5 PM, Monday through Friday.

When are McKinley County property taxes due?

November 10 for the first half and April 10 for the second. Interest starts after December 10 and May 10.

Is trust land in McKinley County taxed by the county?

No. The Bureau of Indian Affairs says trust land is not subject to state or local taxes. Tribes may assess their own taxes, such as the Navajo possessory interest tax.

How long do I have to protest my valuation?

You have 30 days from the date the assessor mailed the notice, or until April 1, whichever is later. File the petition with the county assessor.

Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax that affects a McKinley County estate?

No. New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax, and its estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005.

Can I sell a McKinley County house that has delinquent taxes?

Yes. The tax has to be paid or settled at closing, because the lien ranks ahead of other interests. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer.
